claim: The integrin adhesome contains more than hundred proteins with multiple binding sites for each other.
source: The integrin adhesome contains more than hundred proteins with multiple binding sites for each other (Zamir and Geiger, 2001; Zaidel-Bar et al., 2007; Byron et al., 2011; Kuo et al., 2011; Schiller et al., 2011; Geiger and Zaidel-Bar, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Components of the integrin adhesome get self-assembled along the plasma membrane to form nascent adhesion sites upon local signals.
source: Upon local signals, components of the integrin adhesome get self-assembled along the plasma membrane to form nascent adhesion sites and to further mature them to focal complexes and focal adhesions (Zamir and Geiger, 2001; Cukierman et al., 2002; Gardel et al., 2010; Zaidel-Bar and Geiger, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Adhesion sites assemble, disassemble, and change their molecular content by exchanging their components with the surrounding cytosol.
source: These adhesion sites assemble, disassemble, and change their molecular content by exchanging their components with the surrounding cytosol (Wolfenson et al., 2011; Lavelin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Stationary adhesion sites are dynamically maintained by a balanced rapid exchange of constituents with the cytosol.
source: Likewise, stationary adhesion sites are dynamically maintained by a balanced rapid exchange of constituents with the cytosol (Lele et al., 2008; Wolfenson et al., 2011; Lavelin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The integrin adhesome is extensively pre-assembled already in the cytosol as multi-protein building blocks for adhesion sites.
source: Using fluorescence cross-correlation spectroscopy (FCCS) and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) we found that the integrin adhesome is extensively pre-assembled already in the cytosol as multi-protein building blocks for adhesion sites.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from FCCS and FRAP measurements described in the manuscript

claim: Stationary focal adhesions release symmetrically the same types of protein complexes that they recruit.
source: Stationary focal adhesions release symmetrically the same types of protein complexes that they recruit, thereby keeping the cytosolic pool of building blocks spatiotemporally uniform.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from FCCS measurements near and far from focal adhesions

claim: Multi-protein building blocks enable rapid and modular self-assembly of adhesion sites.
source: We conclude a model in which multi-protein building blocks enable rapid and modular self-assembly of adhesion sites and symmetric exchange of these building blocks preserves their specifications and thus the assembly logic of the system.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and theoretical modeling

claim: Symmetric exchange of building blocks preserves their specifications and thus the assembly logic of the system.
source: We conclude a model in which multi-protein building blocks enable rapid and modular self-assembly of adhesion sites and symmetric exchange of these building blocks preserves their specifications and thus the assembly logic of the system.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data

claim: Among 91 possible pairing combinations of 13 key adhesion site components, 18 protein pairs were found to be physically associated with a p-value <0.0001 in REF52 cells.
source: Among the 91 possible pairing combinations, 18 protein pairs were found to be physically associated with a p-value <0.0001 (Figure 1C,D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by FCCS experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1

claim: Among the 18 protein pairs physically associated in REF52 cells, 15 pairs were found to be physically associated also in NIH3T3 cells with a p-value <0.02.
source: Among these pairs, 15 pairs were found to be physically associated also in the cytosol of another cell line, NIH3T3, with a p-value <0.02 (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by FCCS experimental data in NIH3T3 cells

claim: The assembly of adhesion sites is plausibly carried out by recruitment of pre-assembled multi-protein building blocks, rather than of individual proteins.
source: These results show a strikingly extensive degree of physical associations between adhesion site components in the cytosol. This indicates that the assembly of adhesion sites is plausibly carried out by recruitment of pre-assembled multi-protein building blocks, rather than of individual proteins.
evidence: Inference drawn from the extensive physical associations measured by FCCS

claim: An ILK-PINCH-α-parvin ternary complex exists in the cytosol.
source: Accordingly, by searching for fully intra-connected sub-graphs in the measured network of pairwise physical associations (Figure 1E), two potential ternary complexes can be inferred: an ILK-PINCH-α-parvin complex, which was indeed reported as a ternary complex (Wu, 2004; Legate et al., 2006), and a CAS-FAK-paxillin complex (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by FCCS data showing pairwise associations and confirmed by citations to published literature

claim: A CAS-FAK-paxillin ternary complex potentially exists in the cytosol.
source: Accordingly, by searching for fully intra-connected sub-graphs in the measured network of pairwise physical associations (Figure 1E), two potential ternary complexes can be inferred: an ILK-PINCH-α-parvin complex, which was indeed reported as a ternary complex (Wu, 2004; Legate et al., 2006), and a CAS-FAK-paxillin complex (Figure 1F).
evidence: Inferred from FCCS data showing pairwise associations between these proteins

claim: There is no complex containing more than three of the analyzed proteins.
source: Notably, there is no complex containing more than three of the analyzed proteins.
evidence: Based on analysis of the network of pairwise physical associations measured by FCCS

claim: Cytosolic complexes of the integrin adhesome are considerably confined due to mutual-exclusiveness between protein interactions and allosteric regulations.
source: This indicates that despite the abundant multivalent interactions in the integrin adhesome network, its cytosolic complexes are considerably confined due to mutual-exclusiveness between protein interactions and allosteric regulations.
evidence: Inference from the observation that no complexes larger than three proteins were detected

claim: The associations of vinculin and FAK with paxillin are mutually exclusive.
source: For example, paxillin was found to be physically associated with vinculin and FAK, however, no association was found between vinculin and FAK (Figure 1E,G). This suggests that the associations of vinculin and FAK with paxillin are mutually exclusive and therefore a ternary FAK-paxillin-vinculin complex cannot be formed.
evidence: Inferred from FCCS data showing paxillin associates with both vinculin and FAK, but vinculin and FAK do not associate with each other

claim: Common sites along paxillin mediate its interactions with FAK and vinculin.
source: This inferred mutual exclusive relation is consistent with studies reporting that common sites along paxillin mediate its interactions with FAK and vinculin (Turner and Miller, 1994; Brown et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The associations of VASP with zyxin, α-actinin, and vinculin are mutually exclusive.
source: Similarly, our results suggest mutual exclusiveness between the associations of VASP with zyxin, α-actinin, and vinculin and between the associations of zyxin with VASP and CAS (Figure 1G).
evidence: Inferred from FCCS data showing patterns of associations

claim: The associations of zyxin with VASP and CAS are mutually exclusive.
source: Similarly, our results suggest mutual exclusiveness between the associations of VASP with zyxin, α-actinin, and vinculin and between the associations of zyxin with VASP and CAS (Figure 1G).
evidence: Inferred from FCCS data showing patterns of associations

claim: The size-confinement of cytosolic complexes reflects a system-level design of interdependencies between protein interactions throughout the integrin adhesome network to prevent stochastic assembly of aberrant large complexes.
source: We postulate that the size-confinement of cytosolic complexes reflects a system-level design of interdependencies between protein interactions throughout the integrin adhesome network to prevent stochastic assembly of aberrant large complexes.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed size confinement of cytosolic complexes

claim: ILK-α-parvin, ILK-PINCH, and α-parvin-PINCH are prominent building blocks for focal adhesions.
source: Plotting these co-dynamics distances vs the association scores indicated some protein pairs as prominent building blocks (Figure 2H), including ILK-α-parvin, ILK-PINCH and α-parvin-PINCH (reflecting the trimetric ILK-PINCH-α-parvin complex) (Wu, 2004; Legate et al., 2006), paxillin-vinculin, CAS-FAK, VASP-zyxin, and α-actinin-VASP (Figure 2H).
evidence: Based on combined analysis of FCCS association scores and FRAP dynamics measurements

claim: Paxillin-vinculin is a prominent building block for focal adhesions.
source: Plotting these co-dynamics distances vs the association scores indicated some protein pairs as prominent building blocks (Figure 2H), including ILK-α-parvin, ILK-PINCH and α-parvin-PINCH (reflecting the trimetric ILK-PINCH-α-parvin complex) (Wu, 2004; Legate et al., 2006), paxillin-vinculin, CAS-FAK, VASP-zyxin, and α-actinin-VASP (Figure 2H).
evidence: Based on combined analysis of FCCS association scores and FRAP dynamics measurements

claim: CAS-FAK is a prominent building block for focal adhesions.
source: Plotting these co-dynamics distances vs the association scores indicated some protein pairs as prominent building blocks (Figure 2H), including ILK-α-parvin, ILK-PINCH and α-parvin-PINCH (reflecting the trimetric ILK-PINCH-α-parvin complex) (Wu, 2004; Legate et al., 2006), paxillin-vinculin, CAS-FAK, VASP-zyxin, and α-actinin-VASP (Figure 2H).
evidence: Based on combined analysis of FCCS association scores and FRAP dynamics measurements

claim: VASP-zyxin is a prominent building block for focal adhesions.
source: Plotting these co-dynamics distances vs the association scores indicated some protein pairs as prominent building blocks (Figure 2H), including ILK-α-parvin, ILK-PINCH and α-parvin-PINCH (reflecting the trimetric ILK-PINCH-α-parvin complex) (Wu, 2004; Legate et al., 2006), paxillin-vinculin, CAS-FAK, VASP-zyxin, and α-actinin-VASP (Figure 2H).
evidence: Based on combined analysis of FCCS association scores and FRAP dynamics measurements

claim: α-actinin-VASP is a prominent building block for focal adhesions.
source: Plotting these co-dynamics distances vs the association scores indicated some protein pairs as prominent building blocks (Figure 2H), including ILK-α-parvin, ILK-PINCH and α-parvin-PINCH (reflecting the trimetric ILK-PINCH-α-parvin complex) (Wu, 2004; Legate et al., 2006), paxillin-vinculin, CAS-FAK, VASP-zyxin, and α-actinin-VASP (Figure 2H).
evidence: Based on combined analysis of FCCS association scores and FRAP dynamics measurements

claim: Proteins of prominent building block pairs have similar diffusion speeds in the cytosol.
source: Noteworthy, the proteins of each of these pairs have also similar diffusion speeds, as measured by FCS (Figure 2B,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they are predominantly bound to each other, rather than with other proteins, in the cytosolic pool.
evidence: Supported by FCS measurements of diffusion speeds

claim: Proteins in prominent building block pairs are predominantly bound to each other, rather than with other proteins, in the cytosolic pool.
source: Noteworthy, the proteins of each of these pairs have also similar diffusion speeds, as measured by FCS (Figure 2B,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they are predominantly bound to each other, rather than with other proteins, in the cytosolic pool.
evidence: Inferred from similar diffusion speeds measured by FCS

claim: The cytosolic building blocks of adhesion sites are combinatorially diversified.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the cytosolic building blocks of adhesion sites are combinatorially diversified and that most proteins can be recruited to these sites as part of different types of building blocks.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that physical associations in the cytosol do not necessarily imply similarity in dynamics in adhesion sites

claim: Most proteins can be recruited to adhesion sites as part of different types of building blocks.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the cytosolic building blocks of adhesion sites are combinatorially diversified and that most proteins can be recruited to these sites as part of different types of building blocks.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that physical associations in the cytosol do not necessarily imply similarity in dynamics in adhesion sites

claim: Cytosolic associations between integrin adhesome proteins occur only between proteins from the same functional group and vertical layer, or between proteins from adjacent vertical layers.
source: Superimposing this information with the physical associations found in the cytosol (Figure 1E) shows that such associations occur only between proteins from the same functional group and vertical layer, or between proteins from adjacent vertical layers without including any other analyzed protein in the complex.
evidence: Based on analysis combining FCCS data with published structural information about focal adhesions

claim: The cytosolic building blocks appear to be modules that are continuous along the functional axis of anchoring-mechanosensing-actin regulation and along the vertical axis across focal adhesions.
source: Therefore, the cytosolic building blocks appear to be modules that are continuous along the functional axis of anchoring-mechanosensing-actin regulation and along the vertical axis across focal adhesions.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of associations observed in relation to the vertical organization of focal adhesions

claim: Cell-matrix adhesion sites are dynamically maintained structures that constantly exchange their constituting material with the cytosol.
source: Cell-matrix adhesion sites are dynamically maintained structures that constantly exchange their constituting material with the cytosol (Lele et al., 2008; Wolfenson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In symmetric exchange, proteins exit from adhesion sites with the same state they had upon entering these sites.
source: In a symmetric exchange, proteins exit from adhesion sites with the same state they had upon entering these sites, while in an asymmetric exchange they exit in a different state, termed herein a primed state.
evidence: Definition provided as part of the theoretical framework

claim: In asymmetric exchange, proteins exit from adhesion sites in a different, primed state.
source: In a symmetric exchange, proteins exit from adhesion sites with the same state they had upon entering these sites, while in an asymmetric exchange they exit in a different state, termed herein a primed state.
evidence: Definition provided as part of the theoretical framework

claim: An asymmetric exchange would generate a spatial gradient of primed components emanating from adhesion sites.
source: Therefore, an asymmetric exchange, but not a symmetric exchange, would generate a spatial gradient of primed components emanating from adhesion sites.
evidence: Logical inference from the definition of asymmetric exchange

claim: Both symmetric and asymmetric exchanges allow for a spatiotemporal steady state between adhesion sites and cytosol.
source: Noteworthy, both symmetric and asymmetric exchanges allow for a spatiotemporal steady state between adhesion sites and cytosol.
evidence: Theoretical consideration based on the models

claim: Only an asymmetric exchange enables one adhesion site to affect another one, or itself, via the primed components that it releases to the cytosol.
source: However, only an asymmetric exchange enables one adhesion site to affect another one, or itself, via the primed components that it releases to the cytosol.
evidence: Logical inference from the properties of asymmetric exchange

claim: An asymmetric exchange would generate a locally heterogeneous cloud of building blocks around adhesion sites.
source: An asymmetric exchange would also generate a locally heterogeneous cloud of building blocks around adhesion sites, which may pose an engineering challenge for ensuring correct self-assembly and maintenance of these sites.
evidence: Logical inference from the properties of asymmetric exchange

claim: A symmetric exchange ensures a spatially uniform pool of building blocks for adhesion sites.
source: In contrast, a symmetric exchange ensures a spatially uniform pool of building blocks for adhesion sites and prevents any communication between these sites via primed components.
evidence: Logical inference from the properties of symmetric exchange

claim: A symmetric exchange prevents any communication between adhesion sites via primed components.
source: In contrast, a symmetric exchange ensures a spatially uniform pool of building blocks for adhesion sites and prevents any communication between these sites via primed components.
evidence: Logical inference from the properties of symmetric exchange

claim: For all 28 examined protein pairs, there is no significant difference in association scores near (<1.5 μm) and far from focal adhesions.
source: For all the 28 protein pairs we found no significant difference in association scores near and far from focal adhesions, supporting the model of symmetric exchange of protein complexes (Figure 3B–F; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by FCCS measurements at different distances from focal adhesions

claim: The absence of spatial gradients in protein associations around focal adhesions supports the model of symmetric exchange of protein complexes.
source: For all the 28 protein pairs we found no significant difference in association scores near and far from focal adhesions, supporting the model of symmetric exchange of protein complexes (Figure 3B–F; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Inference from FCCS data showing no spatial gradients

claim: Physical associations near focal adhesions are correlated with their associations far from focal adhesions regardless of their interaction state in focal adhesions.
source: Combining the FCCS measurements with fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) of four protein pairs, we found indeed that the physical associations near focal adhesions are correlated with their associations far from focal adhesions regardless of their interaction state in focal adhesions (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Supported by combined FCCS and FLIM measurements

claim: There are no spatial gradients of different (i.e., primed) protein complexes around focal adhesions.
source: These results indicate that there are no spatial gradients of different (i.e., primed) protein complexes around focal adhesions, indicating that stationary focal adhesions release the same types of complexes that they recruited.
evidence: Inference from FCCS and FLIM data showing no spatial differences in associations

claim: Stationary focal adhesions release the same types of complexes that they recruited.
source: These results indicate that there are no spatial gradients of different (i.e., primed) protein complexes around focal adhesions, indicating that stationary focal adhesions release the same types of complexes that they recruited.
evidence: Inference from FCCS and FLIM data showing no spatial differences in associations

claim: FAK, paxillin, and CAS are tyrosine-phosphorylated proteins in adhesion sites.
source: Therefore, we further tested whether tyrosine-phosphorylated proteins in adhesion sites, such as FAK, paxillin, and CAS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) are recruited and released in different phosphorylation states.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The dSH2 biosensor is enriched in focal adhesions.
source: This reporter is enriched in focal adhesions (Kirchner et al., 2003), where it also exhibits FRET with FAK, paxillin, and CAS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation and FLIM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The dSH2 biosensor exhibits FRET with FAK, paxillin, and CAS in focal adhesions.
source: This reporter is enriched in focal adhesions (Kirchner et al., 2003), where it also exhibits FRET with FAK, paxillin, and CAS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The association scores of CAS, paxillin, and FAK with dSH2 show no significant difference between near and far locations from focal adhesions.
source: The association scores of all three proteins with dSH2 show no significant difference between the near and far locations, indicating that there is no detectable spatial gradient in the phosphorylation level of paxillin, CAS, and FAK around focal adhesions (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: Supported by FCCS measurements with dSH2 biosensor

claim: There is no detectable spatial gradient in the phosphorylation level of paxillin, CAS, and FAK around focal adhesions.
source: The association scores of all three proteins with dSH2 show no significant difference between the near and far locations, indicating that there is no detectable spatial gradient in the phosphorylation level of paxillin, CAS, and FAK around focal adhesions (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: Inference from FCCS measurements with dSH2 biosensor showing no spatial differences

claim: Inhibition of phosphatases by vanadate increases the association scores between dSH2 and CAS, paxillin and FAK.
source: Noteworthy, inhibition of phosphatases by vanadate increases the association scores between dSH2 and CAS, paxillin and FAK, indicating the capability of the assay to detect changes in phosphorylation levels of proteins in the cytosol (Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by FCCS measurements before and after vanadate treatment

claim: The results support the model of symmetric material exchange for stationary focal adhesions.
source: Together, these results support the model of symmetric material exchange for stationary focal adhesions.
evidence: Inference from all FCCS and FLIM data showing no spatial gradients in associations or phosphorylation

claim: Stationary focal adhesions do not alter the cytosolic pool of building blocks.
source: Accordingly, stationary focal adhesions do not alter the cytosolic pool of building blocks and do not communicate or interfere with nearby adhesion sites via primed components.
evidence: Inference from the symmetric exchange model supported by experimental data

claim: Stationary focal adhesions do not communicate or interfere with nearby adhesion sites via primed components.
source: Accordingly, stationary focal adhesions do not alter the cytosolic pool of building blocks and do not communicate or interfere with nearby adhesion sites via primed components.
evidence: Inference from the symmetric exchange model supported by experimental data

claim: Multi-protein building blocks reduce the number of steps required for self-assembly of adhesion sites compared to single-protein building blocks.
source: Multi-protein building blocks, in comparison to single-protein building blocks, reduce the number of steps required for self-assembly of adhesion sites.
evidence: Logical inference from the concept of multi-protein building blocks

claim: With properly designed regulation, reduction of assembly steps can make the self-assembly of adhesion sites less sensitive to stochastic biochemical noise and therefore faster.
source: With a properly designed regulation, such a reduction of steps can make the self-assembly of adhesion sites less sensitive to stochastic biochemical noise and therefore also faster.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the implications of multi-protein building blocks

claim: The regulation of adhesion sites assembly should consider each building block as a whole rather than its constituting proteins as individuals.
source: Since each protein can be a component of different building blocks, this regulation should consider each building block as a whole rather than its constituting proteins as individuals.
evidence: Inference from the observed combinatorial diversity of building blocks

claim: Without considering building blocks as wholes, the self-assembly process would lose control on the identity of the co-recruited proteins and be drifted to form aberrant structures.
source: Otherwise, the self-assembly process would lose control on the identity of the co-recruited proteins when recruiting a protein embedded in a multi-protein building block and thereby will be drifted to form aberrant structures.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the consequences of improper regulation

claim: At the plasma membrane, the system can get locally switched on to self-assemble adhesion sites by passing through checkpoints that induce additional protein interactions in the integrin adhesome.
source: We propose that at the plasma membrane the system can get locally switched on to self-assemble adhesion sites by passing through checkpoints that induce additional protein interactions in the integrin adhesome (Figure 4).
evidence: Proposed model based on inference from experimental data and established knowledge

claim: Assembly checkpoints include mechanical stabilization of the active conformation of matrix-anchored integrin by actin polymerization.
source: These checkpoints include mechanical stabilization of the active conformation of matrix-anchored integrin by actin polymerization (Puklin-Faucher and Sheetz, 2009; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Gardel et al., 2010; Shattil et al., 2010), activation of proteins (e.g., vinculin) at the plasma membrane by phosphatidyl-inositol-4-5-bisphosphate (PIP2) (Gilmore and Burridge, 1996; Zamir and Geiger, 2001), and mechanical stretching of proteins (e.g., talin and CAS) by actomyosin contractility (Riveline et al., 2001; Sawada et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2007; del Rio et al., 2009; Puklin-Faucher and Sheetz, 2009; Gardel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Assembly checkpoints include activation of proteins (e.g., vinculin) at the plasma membrane by PIP2.
source: These checkpoints include mechanical stabilization of the active conformation of matrix-anchored integrin by actin polymerization (Puklin-Faucher and Sheetz, 2009; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Gardel et al., 2010; Shattil et al., 2010), activation of proteins (e.g., vinculin) at the plasma membrane by phosphatidyl-inositol-4-5-bisphosphate (PIP2) (Gilmore and Burridge, 1996; Zamir and Geiger, 2001), and mechanical stretching of proteins (e.g., talin and CAS) by actomyosin contractility (Riveline et al., 2001; Sawada et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2007; del Rio et al., 2009; Puklin-Faucher and Sheetz, 2009; Gardel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Assembly checkpoints include mechanical stretching of proteins (e.g., talin and CAS) by actomyosin contractility.
source: These checkpoints include mechanical stabilization of the active conformation of matrix-anchored integrin by actin polymerization (Puklin-Faucher and Sheetz, 2009; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Gardel et al., 2010; Shattil et al., 2010), activation of proteins (e.g., vinculin) at the plasma membrane by phosphatidyl-inositol-4-5-bisphosphate (PIP2) (Gilmore and Burridge, 1996; Zamir and Geiger, 2001), and mechanical stretching of proteins (e.g., talin and CAS) by actomyosin contractility (Riveline et al., 2001; Sawada et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2007; del Rio et al., 2009; Puklin-Faucher and Sheetz, 2009; Gardel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A standardized pool of building blocks is essential for correct and efficient assembly of adhesion sites.
source: Since adhesion sites are self-assembled structures, a standardized pool of building blocks is essential for their correct and efficient assembly.
evidence: Inference from the self-assembled nature of adhesion sites

claim: Symmetric material exchange between adhesion sites and cytosol ensures that building blocks will enter and exit adhesion sites without being altered.
source: Symmetric material exchange between adhesion sites and cytosol satisfies this requirement by ensuring that building blocks will enter and exit adhesion sites without being altered.
evidence: Inference from the properties of symmetric exchange and experimental data

claim: In mouse embryonic fibroblasts, FAK and vinculin associate with paxillin very close to disassembling focal adhesions but not far away from them.
source: A previous study reported that in mouse embryonic fibroblasts FAK and vinculin associate with paxillin very close to disassembling focal adhesions but not far away from them (Digman et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Disassembling focal-adhesions might exchange material with the cytosol in an asymmetric manner.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to stationary focal adhesions, disassembling focal-adhesions might exchange material with the cytosol in an asymmetric manner.
evidence: Speculative inference based on cited literature about disassembling focal adhesions

claim: A gradient in association strengths between FAK-paxillin and vinculin-paxillin emanating from disassembling focal adhesions supports the asymmetric material exchange model for disassembling adhesions.
source: Yet, this study (Digman et al., 2009) importantly indicates a gradient in association strengths between these proteins emanating from disassembling focal adhesions, supporting in this case the asymmetric material exchange model.
evidence: Inference from cited literature about disassembling focal adhesions

claim: Asymmetric material exchange by disassembling focal adhesions can enable their rapid destruction by breaking them up to relatively bigger pieces.
source: Asymmetric material exchange by disassembling focal adhesions can enable their rapid destruction by breaking them up to relatively bigger pieces, as well as be a mechanism by which they can affect other adhesion sites.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional implications of asymmetric exchange in disassembling adhesions

claim: Asymmetric material exchange can be a mechanism by which disassembling focal adhesions can affect other adhesion sites.
source: Asymmetric material exchange by disassembling focal adhesions can enable their rapid destruction by breaking them up to relatively bigger pieces, as well as be a mechanism by which they can affect other adhesion sites.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional implications of asymmetric exchange in disassembling adhesions

claim: The sensitivity of FCCS enabled measurements at low concentrations of ectopically expressed proteins, comparable to the range of typical endogenous concentrations.
source: The sensitivity of FCCS enabled to perform these measurements at low concentrations of ectopically expressed proteins, comparable to the range of typical endogenous concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by concentration distribution data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The overall distribution of the association scores was skewed to the right as compared to the negative-control measurements.
source: The overall distribution of the association scores was skewed to the right as compared to the negative-control measurements (Figure 1B, top), indicating the presence of physical associations between some of the analyzed proteins in the cytosol.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FCCS data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The right-skewed distribution of association scores indicates the presence of physical associations between some of the analyzed proteins in the cytosol.
source: The overall distribution of the association scores was skewed to the right as compared to the negative-control measurements (Figure 1B, top), indicating the presence of physical associations between some of the analyzed proteins in the cytosol.
evidence: Inference from the statistical distribution of FCCS association scores

claim: In the cytosol, the building blocks cannot form bigger structures due to dependencies between protein interactions.
source: In the cytosol, the building blocks cannot form bigger structures due to dependencies between protein interactions.
evidence: Inference from the observed size confinement of cytosolic complexes

claim: Paxillin and vinculin are physically associated in the cytosol but they do not contain FAK or VASP in their common building block.
source: For example, paxillin and vinculin are physically associated in the cytosol but they do not contain FAK or VASP in their common building block (Figure 2I).
evidence: Based on FCCS data and analysis of association patterns

claim: FAK and paxillin are located in the integrin-signalling layer of focal adhesions.
source: Accordingly, FAK and paxillin are located in the integrin-signalling layer, vinculin is in the force transduction layer and zyxin, VASP, and α-actinin are in the actin regulation layer (Kanchanawong et al., 2010) (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Vinculin is located in the force transduction layer of focal adhesions.
source: Accordingly, FAK and paxillin are located in the integrin-signalling layer, vinculin is in the force transduction layer and zyxin, VASP, and α-actinin are in the actin regulation layer (Kanchanawong et al., 2010) (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Zyxin, VASP, and α-actinin are located in the actin regulation layer of focal adhesions.
source: Accordingly, FAK and paxillin are located in the integrin-signalling layer, vinculin is in the force transduction layer and zyxin, VASP, and α-actinin are in the actin regulation layer (Kanchanawong et al., 2010) (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature
